newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FEATURE - Sri Lanka moves to avert crippling power shortages.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Sri Lanka moves to avert crippling power shortages.

text.p: Sri Lanka should shake off last year's crippling power shortage with the help of emergency power generation plans and good weather ahead, but needs heavy investment to avert future crises, local experts say.
Sri Lanka suffered daily power cuts averaging five hours from March to August 1996, because of low rainfall during the monsoon.
Hydroelectricity provides 84 percent of the Indian Ocean island's total power output of 1,345 megawatts, according to an official of the Ceylon Electricity Board.
CEB, the state monopoly power company, says it has taken steps to tide it over the January to May dry season by adding about 100 megawats of emergency thermal power.
In addition, a tenth of monthly demand was generated outside the CEB grid last year through incentives to industrialists, said D.G. Wijeratne, CEB head of planning.

Central Bank statistics showed industrial exports were hit by the 1996 power crisis. The sector grew by only 10.5 percent in the first 11 months of 1996, down from 14.9 percent in the same period of 1995.
The CEB official said favourable weather conditions expected in 1997 would also play a major part in keeping the country's hydropower generating capacity on track.
LONG TERM SOLUTIONS SOUGHT

Permanent solutions for the country's power needs, which have grown at about eight percent a year in the last two decades, include a 115 megawatt gas turbine plant and a 40 megawatt diesel plant to be ready by mid-1997.
The gas turbine plant which is being built by Italy's Fiat Avio, a unit of Fiat SpA, at a cost of $28 million, is funded entirely by the CEB.
The diesel plant is being built by Germany's MAN B&W Diesel AG, part of the MAN AG group, at a cost of $56 million, and funded jointly by the CEB and Asian Development Bank (ADB).
"Once these two plants are commissioned, we may decommission some of the emergency measures, which are costly since they use auto diesel," Wijeratne said.
The CEB also expects to boost grid power by 17 megawatts when the country's first BOO (build, operate & own) power station, is commissioned in late 1997.
BOO plants are built and owned by foreign investors who receive profit from selling power to the CEB.
The second BOO power station, a 51 megawatt plant by KHD Great Britain, a unit of Germany's Kloeckner-Humboldt-Deutz AG, is due to be commissioned in 1998.

Long-term development plans to expand the national grid include two combined gas-and-fuel plants of 150 megawatts each, and a 300 megawatt coal plant. There are no fixed target years for these projects.
The CEB's intention is to reduce the country's dependency on hydropower plants to 50 percent by the year 2002. There are no plans to build nuclear power plants.
GREATER RELIANCE ON FOSSIL FUELS BRINGS RISKS
But the expansion will come at a cost, Wijeratne said.
"We will be dependent on imported fuel, and like in 1996 if a barrel of diesel rises to $32 from $24, someone will have to pick up the tab, and it certainly won't be the CEB," he said.
The first new hydropower plant which will generate 70 megawatts by damming a tributary of the Kalu Ganga river in the south, will be commissioned by 2002.
Overall, Sri Lanka plans to invest about $2 billion to nearly double its current generating capacity over the next 10 years, with private sector help to prevent a repeat of outages.
Wijeratne said the crippling drought of 1996 was expected to strike again, since weather patterns had shown that severe dry spells occured every four to five years.
"But we could not add a single megawatt since the early 1990s, due to a policy shift by international funding agencies, mainly the World Bank, and delays in the decision-making process."
The World Bank decision to fund infrastructure development through the private sector and local bureaucratic delays in implementing plans led to the 1996 problem, he said.
Apart from planning for an annual load growth of 10 percent which gives a leeway of two percent, the CEB is also moving to cut transmission and distribution losses, now standing at 17 and 19 percent.
"But loss reduction is effective only in the maintenance phase, after the whole country has been given power, whereas only 45 percent of Sri Lanka has electricity," Wijeratne said.
